utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Are the technicians and the interpreters ready? Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the case is IT-95-14/1-T, The Prosecutor versus Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dubuisson. Today we have before us for the Prosecution Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Meddegoda and Ms. Erasmus, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: And for the Defence, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I am Goran Mikulicic, and myself and Srdan Joka shall be for the Defence -- appear for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Very well. We'll resume with this matter. I think we have today before us a witness for the Defence. Is that not right, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your lordships, we shall begin to bring in witnesses. And our first witness is Dr. Vesna Bilic. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Vesna Bilic. Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I ask that you read the solemn declaration, which the court usher will now show to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Bilic, you may now be seated. You will now respond to the questions put to you by Mr. Mikulicic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Bilic.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am with my colleague, Mr. Joka. I am the lawyer for the accused Zlatko Aleksovski. You will be the witness before this Honourable Court, and we shall ask you some questions, and we should like to ask you to answer them to the best of your knowledge and ability. Dr. Bilic, will you please state for the court the date and place of your birth?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 24th of November, 1957 in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What is your ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I am a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you a practicing believer?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What is your faith?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I am a Roman Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us something about your education?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the pharmaceutical faculty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And after the graduation you got a job where?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Immediately at the health centre in Busovaca as a biochemist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And throughout the time to this day you are still with the health centre in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, in what capacity did you work at the Busovaca Health Centre and something about your career?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: In the beginning I worked as a biochemist in the diagnostic laboratory of the health centre in Busovaca, and as of 1991 I'm the director of the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We are making the short breaks because of the interpreters, so would you please slow down so the interpreters can keep up with you. So, as of 1991 you had the health centre at Busovaca. Will you tell us, briefly, what does the -- what are the duties and responsibilities of the director of the health centre?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, the director of the health centre is responsible for the complete -- for the whole activity of the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you -- can you remember how -- what was the staff, how large was the staff in the former half of 1993, roughly?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, roughly -- when did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: 1993, during the conflicts.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: '93. About 30. I think that was the staff altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And who were the personnel?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, roughly, I think six physicians; of them two specialists, one stomatologist, biochemist, that is myself as a director, and some 15 other people of paramedics of different profiles. That includes nurses, the midwives, x-ray technicians, and some auxiliary personnel, drivers, ambulance car and (unclear).

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was it the only medical care institution in Busovaca municipality?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what is the size of the population who used the services of the health centre, roughly, how many patients?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Before the war, some 18.000 individuals used the services of this health centre. Afterwards, I just don't know. I cannot give you any figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what kind of health services did the health centre in Busovaca extend?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: The health centre in Busovaca provided primary health care.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that means?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Primary health care involves the population health care without hospital beds, so we do not -- we only had outpatients. We did not have any hospitalised patients there. It was organised as a gynaecological service, an obstetrical service. We had paediatrician, paediatrician care, general health care, then the emergency aid with all the accompanying services, that is laboratories for diagnostics, x-ray diagnostics and dentistry surgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, you said that you had no hospital beds there, you could not admit anyone for hospitalisation. So if you came across such a case, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: The health care centre in Busovaca then did whatever it could, and in specific conditions then referred those such cases to other hospitals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, which were the hospitals that the health centre at Busovaca referred patients needing hospital treatment?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: At that time, that is in early 1993, it was only the hospital at Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And the Zenica Hospital, did you keep any contact with the Zenica Hospital before the war and in early 1993?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Before the war and in early 1993. Before the war the health centre was part of the regional medical centre in Zenica. However, in early January, when the conflict broke out, we could not get there because the roads were closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, what equipment did the health centre have there for the primary health care? Do you think, as an expert, was this equipment adequate, were there some shortcomings, or did you have enough of what you needed?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: In my personal opinion, before the war the equipment was very poor. And in early war, or in the beginning of the conflict in '93, and in'92, the health centre was shelled straight away, so the whole wing of the whole centre was destroyed. The power and water supply were also cut off, were destroyed. The working conditions were very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You say that in 1992 the health centre was shelled. Could you please explain to the Court what it was?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: It was bombed, that is the Municipality of Busovaca was bombed and two shells or missiles hit the health centre. It was the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So the building was bombed by the former JNA Air Force?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When did it happen?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: It happened in April '92.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You say that at that time a part of the building, of the health centre, was practically devastated?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did some equipment perish?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, the gynaecological surgery was destroyed and the dentistry surgery was destroyed. But we had trouble with water supply, because missiles fell right in front of the building of the health centre and hit the water pipe, so that we were left without water for quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But otherwise, could you tell us how many ambulance cars did the health centre have?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: At the time the health centre had only two cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were they properly equipped? Was there enough fuel, spare parts and everything else?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: These were very old vehicles. I think they were not less than about ten years old. And as for the fuel for ambulance cars, we had difficult time in getting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you please describe the situation with the fuel? Could you readily go out into the field, in view of the state of the vehicles and fuel, or was it more -- rendered more difficult?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: It was really difficult and we used them only in particularly severe cases to transport them to the hospital at Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that in this first half of 1993, when -- therefore in the Municipality of Busovaca, the army conflict broke out, is it then correct to say the health centre could not then go out with the ambulance cars into the field and work there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: We could, but we had a very hard time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, at that time -- I am all the time referring to this former half of '93, so at the time what were the supplies? Did you have enough medicines, food, electricity, water?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: At the time all forms of supplies were very bad, medicines and medical supplies came from all pre-war reserves, all pre-war stocks, because we had some stocks and a little -- and we were donated also a little bit, that is, these were donations from our people working abroad. But it was very difficult. All the supplies -- the delivery was very difficult because we were locked in, closed in. Food deliveries were also very difficult. What there was in the Municipality of Busovaca, we distribute among themselves and consumed among themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You say it was very difficult to come by all that you needed. You said you were locked in. What does that mean? Would you please explain it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, it means that we could not get out from the territory of the Municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Why couldn't you get out of the territory of the Municipality of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Because they were firing at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, you mentioned that as regards food supplies you ate the same kind of food in the Municipality of Busovaca. Where was that prepared?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, that food was prepared in the barracks for all the people, for all people who were under labour directives, under labour obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us who does it refer -- whom do you mean? You said all people who were under labour obligation. You mean the health institution? Who else? What other services or institutions?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Were all the services that had to do work, that is civil defence, prison, the municipal services.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So this food was prepared in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And then it was distributed from there to various points?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, you mentioned that the -- as a result of the bombing by JNA in April 1992, you had difficulties with water supply. Could you tell us something about electricity. How about the power supply?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Likewise, I mean, the same situation. It was very difficult. However, the health centre was fortunate enough that nearby the Dutch battalion was quartered and we were switched onto their generators so that the health centre in Busovaca had electricity throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said the Dutch battalion. You mean UNPROFOR forces?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you cooperate with UNPROFOR units there, apart from being switched onto their power generator?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, if we needed some medicine urgently, or if there was a doctor, a physician in the Dutch battalion, or a nurse, we could always get the particular medicine without any problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But they had their own medical service, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, when the armed conflicts started in '93, could you tell us when was it, roughly, when the first conflict -- when did the first conflict take place?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: The first conflict took place on the 21st of January '93, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what was it? Why do you remember that date?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Why? Well, it was a kind of a conflict between two sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What two sides and what kind of conflict? Of course you know that.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a conflict between the Muslim and the Croat side. It was in the morning -- it began at six o'clock in the morning. I knew nothing about it. I was at home. And only around eight o'clock could I make my way to the health centre, because fire came from all sides. And only the emergency service was at the health centre working. People stayed there and worked for 48 hours and they needed another shift, they needed to be replaced, but it was very difficult to get to the building because of the fire. But somehow we managed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us where did the fire come from? What direction?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: The health centre was fired at from above the health centre. That is where the fire came from, from the village, from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What is the name of the village?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Hodzica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know who lived in that village, what was the ethnic origin of the population?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: They were different. There were Muslims and there were Croats too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, what was the ethnic structure of the employed or the personnel at the health centre at the time, before the conflict, on the eve of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: The health centre, the ethnic structured varied. About 45 percent were Muslims, and Croats also accounted for about 45 percent and the rest were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if you noticed some strange phenomenon and unusual situation prior to the conflict, in view of the personnel of the health centre?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I noticed it only after the conflict broke out, because the majority of the personnel who were of Muslim origin went on holidays at the time, and I had signed their leaves. That is, I allowed them to go and leave. And after the conflict broke out, I noticed that a majority of employed of the Muslim -- of Muslim origin were on holidays or had asked for days off or something. But, at any rate, they were not in the health centre, available at the health centre when the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you try to interpret this afterwards?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How did you interpret that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, evidently something was about to happen that I knew -- had nothing about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And do you think that they knew about it when they were leaving on holidays?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, that was my personal impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, during those -- during the fighting, during the conflict, how was the service organised? How did the health centre function?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: It was very difficult because there were very few physicians, so we had only the emergency service working. We had two physicians working per day around the clock. And since there were few -- I mean, we took shifts every second day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what about the nurses?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: There were slightly more in number. They worked in teams of three or possibly four and they also took shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, at that time what kind of health services did you offer to your patients, and what kind of patients would come to seek medical help to your institution?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: The patients who came to our health centre came from the territory of the Municipality of Busovaca. They were the people who at the time needed some kind of medical help.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you differentiate between categories of patients according to the degree of emergency or some other criteria?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: The only criteria that can be applied is the degree of emergency. We couldn't apply any other criteria.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, since the health centre in Busovaca was the only medical institution in the area at the time, what kind of obligations did you have in terms of epidemiological protection? Could you explain the role of the medical centre in that sense?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: There has to be a department for epidemiological in each health centre, because everything that is happening at the municipality should be actually the work of that particular department. If, in case of diseases, the health centre is immediately advised of the situation, and they send out their team into the field to check out the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Of course you had such type of service organised in your health centre even prior to the breakout of the conflict. Do you remember whether in your area of responsibility were any particular phenomena that were developing at that time, any particular cases that you had to intervene?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, before the conflict there were no epidemics. We had cases of hepatitis or jaundice, but it was only occasionally. It was not something that we had to worry about at the time. And in the area between Busovaca and Vitez there is a village where we had very often, perhaps maybe every four or five years, we would have a case of typhoid fever. But at that time we didn't have any such concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether in -- during the relevant times, that is the first half of 1993, was the situation different in any way? Did you have any cases of infectious diseases, something that would involve epidemiological prevention?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, no not before the conflict or at the beginning of conflict. The situation did not get worse in that respect because the health institution, the health centre in Busovaca was very active in that regard and we had numerous missions in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, you told us that communication was very difficult at that time, and that the supplies were not very good. Does that include clothes and footwear as well, and how did the population cope with that situation?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, they managed to cope with the situation, but sometimes the civilian population also had to put on military clothes, military footwear, uniforms and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that it was normal for the civilian population to wear parts of military clothing at that time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How did they obtain that military clothes?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, do you know anything about medical services that were offered to the detainees of the Kaonik facility at the time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the Kaonik facility was, what kind of facility was it? What was there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: The Kaonik facility was a kind of prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what it was before?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: It was a JNA facility, the Yugoslav Peoples Army facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When did you, you personally and the health centre in Busovaca in general, when did you first come across patients who needed medical help and who were from the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I believe that it happened in the second half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The second half of 1992, what kind of patients were these people, people coming from the Kaonik facility? Do you know anything about them?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, the majority of them were Serbs and Croats of Serbian and Croatian ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify my question, do you know what statutes they had at the Kaonik facility, who were these people?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were they guards, detainees, or maybe civilians that happened to be there, do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, after the conflict broke out you said it was on the 25th of January, 1993. So after that time, when did you first come across people who needed medical help and who were from the Kaonik facility? Did you come across such people?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I, did it was the end of January and the beginning of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And who were these people, could you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: What exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who were the persons that came to your facility -- no, I withdraw that question. Let me ask you the following. Who brought persons from the Kaonik facility to your health centre?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, these people were brought by guards and sometimes by the chief of the prison, by the warden of the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the warden, do you know who that person was?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What's his name?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you recognise him in this room?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you please, for the record, point to the person that you recognise as Zlatko Aleksovski? Could the record please reflect that the witness has pointed to the accused. Dr. Bilic, when did you first meet Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski, did you know him before these events that took place at the beginning of 1993?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know him before that, and I met him, I don't remember the exact date, but it was in late January, early February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you remember the circumstances in which this meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Aleksovski, as the warden of the prison, came to a meeting, to my office. We were supposed to agree on the ways and types of medical protection for the persons who were detained in the prison facility. We wanted to establish whether we can admit these people, on what conditions and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Of course you cannot remember the exact date, you told us it was in late January, beginning of February. But could you tell us whether this was before the break out of conflict or after the conflict?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: It was immediately after the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, do you remember how Mr. Aleksovski was dressed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I couldn't exactly tell you how he was dressed. Sometimes he would wear military shirts and military trousers and sometimes he also worry civilian jacket or shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if he, when he worry parts of military uniform, if he had any insignia on that clothes, any military insignia?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that he came to a meeting with you so that you can agree on types of medical services to be offered to these people, what exactly did you agree upon?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but I know we were discussing conditions, general conditions at that time and I remember that we agree that people could be brought as patients at any time from the Kaonik facility to the health centre in Busovaca around the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That was the type of organisation you have in general all the time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who would bring patients from Kaonik to the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, I was not directly involved with patients, but very often I saw guards bringing people in and a few times I saw Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski. He also brought patients from the prison to the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were you ever present when a vehicle would come to the health centre and when these patients were brought into the building, did you see something like that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What kind of vehicle was that? A vehicle that brought patients from Kaonik to the medical centre, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remembered that that vehicle was always in better condition than our emergency vehicles. As for the specific type and model of the vehicle, I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was it a car or a lorry?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: There used to be a car on several occasions, but sometimes they would also bring people in a van.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, these people who were brought to the health centre for treatment, were they handcuffed, were they tied up, was their freedom of movement was restricted in any way?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: As I already told you, I was not working directly with the patients, so I couldn't observe that. But sometimes in passing as much as I could see, I don't think that they were tied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see what kind of procedure was followed when they were brought to the health centre? Would they also wait in the waiting room as other patients or was it organised in some other way? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know what kind of procedure it was, but I believe that if the physician was available, if we didn't have, if he didn't have another patient, I think that these persons could be immediately admitted to the physician's office. If the physician was busy with some other patient, then I presume they would have to wait in the waiting room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This means that they would be in the waiting room waiting alongside other patients?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, what was the general condition of health of these people who were brought from Kaonik to the health centre, what was your impression when you saw them as patients? Judging by the way they looked were they in any way different from other patients who sought medical health at your institution and I refer to their physical appearance, the way they looked and so on.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, I never noticed any particular, anything particular that would draw my attention, I mean these people were dressed normally as all of us. They appear to me normal. I didn't notice anything particular, any deviations from what was normal at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of complaints they had? What kind of medical problems they had and what kind of help and treatment was offered to them?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, since I am not a physician, I cannot be very specific. I just know that they suffered from some chronic diseases and complained of such diseases as far as I know. Things like high pressure, ulcer, some kind of chronic diseases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, did you recognise amongst these people any one to whom your medical centre had offered services prior to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would recognise from time to time a number of such people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can we therefore say that they were your regular patients?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And that they suffered from some chronic disease?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were just regular patients and most of them were known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, you mentioned that your medical centre, as the only medical institution in the area, was also responsible for the epidemiological and sanitary situation in the area?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you have any such interventions at Kaonik as a medical institution?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Mr. Aleksovski came to see us on one occasion and he asked us to send epidemiological disease control team to the facility at Kaonik so that they would carry out a disinfection of the premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was that carried out?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I remember that that was conducted on two occasions and I was present on -- at one particular occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, you said on two occasions. What period of time do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember exactly, I think it was in February, and maybe two or three months later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Therefore we are talking about the year 1993 all the time. As the head of the medical centre and the person responsible for the epidemiological situation in the field, were you aware at the time that at the Kaonik facility there were cases of skin disease and something similar that you would have to react to?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of that. In case that there were such cases at the time, of course, we would have been advised of that. They would have -- they should have informed of us that. But I was never informed of such problems, therefore, I presume that there weren't any in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you say you were not informed, who do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, I am referring to all the medical personnel from the epidemiological service, people who went there, to carry, to conduct the disinfection. They didn't notice anything improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, you said that you once went to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did go to Kaonik myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when it was?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you the exact date, but I believe it was on the first occasion when we went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I think you mentioned February, 1993?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you describe that visit to Kaonik, was it the first time that you went to Kaonik or had you been there before?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, it was the first time. For me the situation was normal bearing in mind the conditions in the territory of the Municipality of Busovaca at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, could you tell us more about that visit, why did you go there, who invited you, who took you there and where exactly did you go and what was the kind of situation that you found there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: When Mr. Aleksovski came to the health centre and when we asked for our help, when he asked the medical service to check the epidemiological situation at the prison facility, we went there, there was a team of people who went there and I was with them. We went there by car. It was our vehicle belonging to the medical centre. We went to that facility, we had a tour of all premises of the facility and we carried out disinfection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember which particular building you visited?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: We saw every building of the facility, including premises where people were detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, as an expert, what was the epidemiological situation in these premises?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I believe that the situation was normal. If you have in mind the prevailing conditions in Busovaca. I don't think it was any different from what was normal at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: During that visit, did you come across any medical phenomena that would point out the cases of some skin disease, for example lice and other types of infectious diseases?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't find any such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can I therefore say it was some kind of preventative action?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, did you have an opportunity to inspect toilets?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. And the toilets were normal. I mean they were just like other rooms, other premises of that facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you be more specific, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean that it was not dirty. That it was -- I don't know what else to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was there anything particular, anything that would be alarming to you as an employee of the health centre?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, no. There was no need for us to react in such sense. We just had this simple action that we had to conduct in order to prevent the spreading of skin diseases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Am I correct, therefore, in thinking that such type of preventative actions were always conducted by your institution on places where a number of people were accommodated together?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was the normal type of action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell whether there were any other such facilities in the territory of your municipality where similar actions were conducted?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, we did the same everywhere, in all places where a number of people were put together. For example, in refugee centres, in kitchens where food was prepared for a large number of people and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, when you were at Kaonik at the time did you have opportunity to see people who were detained there? Did you see any of them?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you speak with them?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said you saw them, could you describe the condition they were in to the best of your recollection? It was a long time ago, I know.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that their condition was normal for the type of facility they were in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you notice any cases of malnutrition?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you notice, perhaps, cases of neglect of physical appearance?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What about their clothes and footwear, were they in any worse condition than the general condition in the area?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can I, therefore, conclude that these people appeared to you as everybody else in that particular area, that particular time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you see any visible injuries? Any wounded people?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice any such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, did you at any later point, I mean after February 1993, did you visit Kaonik or was it, or was that the only occasion that you went there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: That was the only occasion I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What about your personnel, your staff?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, they went there once again to conduct fumigation and very often people would be treated at home. I mean, doctors, physicians, would go to the Kaonik facility with a nurse to conduct medical examination if it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was it something extraordinary or was it normal, usual practice?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: It was usual if the physician was available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic at the beginning of your testimony you mentioned that your medical facility was in charge of primary health care and whenever you would come across a patient whose condition required specialist approach, you would refer such patients to hospitals in Zenica and then afterwards in Nova Bila when the roads were closed. Do you remember an occasion when you transported or sent patients to Zenica in your ambulance car? Do you remember any such event?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I remember that on the day when the conflict broke out, that is the 25th of January, 1993, I remember that we drove, I mean the driver of the medical centre, he took a couple of patients to Zenica to hospital. After that, he would return from the Zenica hospital without patients. But on one occasion he was stopped, he was harassed and the ambulance was taken away from him. He was stopped at a checkpoint, I believe it was a Muslim checkpoint, so it was the Muslims then who stopped him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what happened to the driver?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: They harassed him for about two or three hours. He was with those men and then they released him and he walked for awhile and then found somebody to give him a lift to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what about the ambulance car?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: They seised it and we never learned about its whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After that event, did you ever transport your patients to Zenica? Was it possible?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, it was not and we did not dare because we were left with only one ambulance car, so if even if we did send it and passed all those checkpoints we could then lose that one car. So we stopped sending them there, we continued to refer them to the hospital at Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what kind of patients did you refer to hospitals, what were their complaints?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I don't really remember what were the health problems, but I think it was a mere cardiac infraction or hypertension or something, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, at the time, did your health care centre also treat HVO soldiers? Did they come to the health centre?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did, because it was the only medical institution which could treat patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you notice anything amongst HVO soldiers which had to be treated?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, whatever we could do. And we could not treat them further, then we referred them to the Nova Bila Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we are talking about HVO men. Did you have any instances of extending treatment or helping or seeing a soldier with the markings HV, not HVO?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: During all these events did you ever see some soldiers with the markings HV?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. Personally, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, during all the while that we are referring to, and that is the first half of '93, did you have any contact with Zlatko Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Quite often when Mr. Aleksovski would come along, then we would greet one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But apart from the first understanding about services rendered, did you have any more of such things?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I can't remember all the details and all the time he visited us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you describe -- could you tell us something about the frequency of these?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps once a week or once a fortnight or once in ten days. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Apart from these personal contacts, could you also communicate by telephone?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you then communicate by telephone?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: We did, when necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, did the health services extended by your health centre vary between, shall I call them civilian patients and those who came from the Kaonik facility, did these standards vary as to the treatment?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No. There was no difference because it is simply inadmissible in health services.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, those patients who came from Kaonik, you said they had some chronic, they suffered from some chronic ailments mostly. You must have been prescribing some treatment for them and medicines. Now, how was that organised?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: How the health centre organised it. Well, if a patient came to us with -- complaining of a chronic disease, then we, that is the physicians, would prescribe their treatment, and it was provided to a patient at the health centre if it concerned some injections or something else, or if not, there was also a pharmacy at the health centre, so that we would issue them pills or whatever for these patients. Or for those people from Kaonik, we gave them to the guards so they would administer those medicines to them at prescribed times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, you mentioned that at that time there were how many physicians did you say?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: At that time there were six physicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who that was?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Dr. Nada Petrovic, Dr. Dragica Akrap-Raos, Dr. Srdjana Markovic, Dr. Bernardica Mioc, Dr. Zvonimir Stipac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Many of these colleagues, are they still with the health centre or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are. Dr. Petrovic is there. She is a gynaecologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Raos Akrap and Dr. Stipec Zvonimir and Dr. Bernardica Mioc and Srdjana Markovic are not there any longer?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, they are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know when a particular service rendered to patients either from Kaonik or other cases, did those -- did the physicians provide some documentation, I mean prescriptions or some case history, a paper where they would write out the diagnosis?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was -- I mean, it was on record, but we had so many problems that we did not have the proper forms. But somehow we did find time to put a record, all the patients who came to see us. And since we had our pharmacy for oral medicines, then naturally, of course, we had to justify these prescriptions. So physicians had to issue prescriptions which they -- with which the patients that went to the pharmacy and that those prescriptions were kind of a certificate that a particular medicine had been issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, I shall show you now some of the documents, doctoral documents, the documents issued by doctors, and I shall ask you to comment on them; that is, tell me if they were issued by people who worked at the health centre at the time, and what kind of complaints are referred to in these documents. Dr. Bilic, I shall ask you now that you try to read each one of these documents. They are written in -- you know, in the notorious doctors handwriting which nobody can read apart from their authors. But can you please try to do that and tell us what it is about.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Ilijas Krivosija, 1942. That must be the year of his birth. Yes. Diagnosis, herniated disk. Spared from work and flat cot, flat bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who issued it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: It was Dr. Mioc who issued it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: She was in the employ of the health centre?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can proceed to the second document. So this is a document D18.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the first time we've seen these documents and there is no indication of what period they relate to, from what I can see. Some of them may do, but certainly the document we just looked at doesn't. What relevance it is -- I mean, if it's not relating to anyone from Kaonik, I fail to see the relevance of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Lordships. I shall ask the witness if she could tell us what timeframe do they pertain to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, looking at this first document, could you identify the patient; that is, do you know where he came from and what time period does it refer to?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can, because I know that particular patient personally, and this was this time, the first or the second day of the conflict, since the outbreak of the conflict. So this could have been the 25th of January or the 26th of January 1993, because Dr. Bernardica Mioc was on duty at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. And will you please try to do the same with every other document that you go through. If you can, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. Are you now satisfied with the response, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, no, Your Honour, because I have no idea if it has any connection whatsoever to Kaonik. Your Honours, there may be a reason outside of giving treatment to people who weren't in Kaonik, if Mr. Mikulicic would care to develop that, then I probably would be able to remove my objection. But at the moment it looks as though it's just a medical form in relation to somebody in the area, it would seem, at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic and Mr. Niemann, I believe we arrived at a time where we might take a recess. I believe that Mr. Mikulicic could, before presenting these documents, state and inform us, because as the Prosecution has just stated, it is seeing this document for the first time. So perhaps it would be appropriate to state that with this document I wish to prove such and such thing. And then at that point say that, for all of us, that the document be presented on the ELMO so that all of us can be able to follow the reading then by Dr. Bilic. Having made that proposal, I think we might then take a 20 minute recess and then resume with that proposal. If you are in agreement with that. Very well, 20 minutes. --- Proceedings recessed at 10.45 a.m. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Very well, now let us resume. Before doing so, I would like to tell you that next Wednesday the Tribunal will be sitting in the afternoon. So we're going to be keeping the same time. It will be from 13.30 until 17.30. Mr. Mikulicic and Mr. Niemann, if it is appropriate or convenient for you rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Mikulicic, regarding our last proposal, will it be possible to resume on that note? I think in that way, Mr. Niemann then will withdraw his objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, let me first thank you for the kind suggestion to the Defence in connection with the documents we proposed. I will gladly accept it. Let me first state the purpose as to why we wanted to introduce these documents. Our objective was for the witness, on the basis of her recollection and her knowledge of certain patients. We must bear in mind that it was a small town where people knew each other very well, so that she can therefore confirm whether these people were patients who had been brought to Kaonik for purposes of medical treatment or not. This is one thing. The other thing is that the Defence wants to show with these documents that medical services were also offered to Muslims, because all these people are of Muslim ethnic origin. We want to show that no other standards were applied. And also on the basis again of the recollection of the witness, we would like to show that these documents were issued at that particular time in cases where the document does not bear a specific date. If the witness can remember, of course. If she doesn't, she will say so. I don't know whether my explanation is satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann. Do you have anything you would like to add generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On the basis of their merely to demonstrate that they were Muslim patients who were treated along with other patients, we don't have any objection to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you for your understanding and cooperation. You may now resume, Mr. Mikulicic, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I can ask the assistance of the usher in accordance with the suggestion of the Chamber, can the document 18-A be placed on the ELMO, please. We can all see what document we are referring to. Dr. Bilic, can we come back to this document and could you tell us if you personally know the patient by the name of Ilijas Krivosija?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know him, he was my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On the basis of this particular document, do you know when this document was issued and do you know where Mr. Krivosija was at the time this document was issued?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I know that this document was issued at the health centre in Busovaca. There is no date on the document, but I believe it was on the 25th or 26th of January, 1993, when Dr. Bernardica Mioc was on duty, together with Dr. Nada Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether this patient was brought to the health centre from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember he was brought from the Kaonik prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The therapy that was recommended for this particular patient, does that remind you of anything? What does it tell you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: This means that this patient was supposed to be taken back by the people who have brought him to the health centre and that this therapy should be provided to him at the prison facility. Because this was necessary in view of his diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us once again what diagnosis it was?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Herniated disk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Chamber whether this a chronic disease or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I am not a physician, but I think it was a chronic disease.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now move on to the next document, please. Again, Dr. Bilic, could you give us some information about this document. How would you comment this particular document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know this patient. But I can say that because of the therapy that was recommended here, house treatment, I think that he was a prison detainee. Because why else would the physician put here house treatment if the patient was at home?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we move on to the next document, please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document D-18/B.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Document 18 or 19?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, no, with regard to all of these, we're referring to document D-18/A, B, C and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, this document was issued for the patient by the name Smet Medjuseljac, do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know him not personally, but I knew him. He used to be a high school teacher in Busovaca before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What kind of disorders or illnesses did he suffer from?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Again, I am not a physician, but judging from the diagnosis that's mentioned here, I think he suffered from ulcer, duodenal ulcer. Therapy is indicated here. Again, the patient should be seated or should lie on a flat surface. And I think that this particular patient was also one of the Kaonik detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who issued this particular document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Dr. Petrovic Nada who was together on duty with Dr. Mioc during these days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What time period are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: It must have been on the 25th or 26th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, can we move on to the next document, please. Dr. Bilic, the same question as before.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: This is Ejub Buljina, diagnosis is a 4 to 5, I don't know exactly which type of classification this is. I believe this is the old international classification of diseases. And, again, the therapy that is indicated here, house treatment for the duration of five days at least. This means that the doctor recommended that the patient should go home and spend five days at home for treatment. That is that he should be released from prison for the duration of five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when this was issued and who issued this document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: It was Dr. Markovic Srdjana, surgeon, but I cannot remember the exact date. However, I believe that it was at the beginning of the conflict, the 27th or the 28th of January, when this particular doctor was on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: With regards to this documents on Indictments 425, that will be D-18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: No, no, D.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be D.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, could you please have a look at this document and make some comments. We have a date here.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: As far as I can read it this is 25th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know the patient?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: The patient is Suad Halilovic. I know him by sight. And the diagnosis, as far as I can read it, thoracical contusions or something like that, a blow in the chest without fracture. So if doctor has put here "without fracture," it means that there should be an x-ray as well, x-ray of the chest, patient's chest, because she indicated "without fracture." She must have seen somehow that there was no fracture and the therapy indicated is house treatment as well. So once again, I can conclude that he was in prison and that he was sent by the doctor for house treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Next document, please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Be document D-18/E.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Hasim Pezic, do you know him?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you comment on this document, please, and tell us about the time it was issued?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, the document is 4, 5, 4, the old international classification of diseases again. And I don't know which particular disease this is. Therapy recommended is cold compresses and home treatment again. So once again, I think we can conclude that this patient was sent for home treatment from Kaonik. The doctor who wrote this, because of the time when she was on duty, I believe that the exact date would be either 25th or 26th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Next document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Will be given the number D-18/F.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Nasib Silajdzic, do you know him?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Please, can we have your comment as to the medical treatment that is indicated in this document, time when the document was issued and where was the person when he required medical help?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: We have here swelling, left ear. The left ear, I can't read this. Ortho H is prescribed, ear drops and we have a note here, the patient should avoid draught, should be sent home for treatment and, therefore, I can conclude that the patient was from Kaonik and it was sent to home treatment by the person who issued a document, who signed the document, Dr. Bernardica Mioc who was on duty on the 25th or 26th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can we move on to the next document please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Document D-18/G.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We have a document on the 26th of January, '93, signed by Dr. Bernardica Mioc and this person is Senad Dervic, do you know this individual?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know this individual personally because we were colleagues. This patient worked at the health care administration so that we cooperated very closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In Busovaca you mean?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Busovaca. I know him personally. And according to this diagnosis, 5-P 3, 2, I don't know what it means because I am not a doctor, but at any rate it is a genital ulcer evidently. And the treatment is Eglonyl ampule so that the patient could be administered it at the health centre. And then Belamet tablets (check medication name). The patient should be trussed and treatment at home. Dr. Bernardica Mioc issued this prescription and she was on duty on the 26th of January. I remember this patient exactly because I knew him well and because we were associates. We cooperated and I know that he was brought from Kaonik there. That I took him into my office and that I gave him a package of cigarettes and that he was sent home for treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document concerning Senad Dervic will be given D-19/H.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Ethem Lusija, do you know this individual?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where is he from?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: From Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you comment on this document the same as before. So it was signed by Dr. Nada Petrovic. Can you tell us when this was and whether this person was in Kaonik at that time as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: At that time, Dr. Nada Petrovic, as I said, was on duty together with Dr. Mioc, so this document could have been issued on the 25th or 26th of January, 1993. She measured his pressure, blood pressure twice, 220 through to 200 and 200 through 125. So it must be a heart case, a cardiac patient. Because evidently, she did EEG, that is, ECG and see how the heart functioned because she could see that the heart beat was fastened but there was no noise either in systaltic pressure or anywhere. And the other thing she could do only after the electrocardiogram. And she prescribed this treatment Lasix ampule which is a sedative pills, Aldomet pills -- oh, it says tablets. Two times one. When this patient was brought in, she measured his pressure, did the electrocardiography, prescribed the medicines, waited for the patient to have his pressure measured once again and it was 200 through 125. After that she prescribed pills and she must have asked people who had brought in this patient to enable him to be assigned treatment at home. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you conclude from that that this person was brought from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be document D-18/I.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, concerning the objection I originally raised. The date on this document appears to me to be 1991. If it is 1991, I then I don't see the relevance of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, it is true that the date on here is 27 January 1991 and so this is outside the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a document which in the translation date of issue 27 January '91. The prescription is in handwriting. And if you look at the original of the prescription, you will see that a figure after figure 9 could be 3 just as well as it can be 1. So that I should like to ask the doctor to use the same methodology she used to interpret the other document to try to interpret this one. And to see whether this document was indeed issued in '91 as it said in translation into English and French. Or is it the date which transpires from the original document. Sir, could the witness comment. And if this is indeed a document of '91, then I will not propose it as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I certainly have no objection of the witness being questioned on it, Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Okay. Very well, Mr. Mikulicic excuse me. Thank you, Mr. Niemann. Please resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, we have a document, could you please describe to the Court what document is this?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: It's different from others. This document, this is the original prescription which the physicians issued for the pharmacy so that patients could get this medicine. The only difference is that if this prescription were of '91 as this figure down there looks like, then I think they should have filled in all the columns in this prescription. And one does not see it here. Because we have the name Hasan Pezic, addressed Busovaca. That the document was -- had this document been issued in '91, they would have had to also add the personal number in full. Because in '91 all patients had to come to the health centre, to be covered by the health care, they had to bring in their health certificates. And these health certificates included all the data, that is, the number, the register number, the personal number of the patient in question with the diagnosis and everything else. And such a prescription in '91 would not be recognised by any pharmacy, by any chemist because it was not filled out properly. So it could have been issued at the time. Perhaps it was written by hand and a mistake was made, 27th of January. I think the doctor, surgeon, Srdjana Markovic was employed by the health centre at the time and perhaps the patient did not have his health card, health certificate with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, there is one element in regards to the number in this document, and also in the following document there is a number series indicated on this document, and from this series you can see that it is the same. My colleague, Judge Vohrah, drew my attention to this fact. Therefore, we have a document before us which has the date '91 indicated, but the following document is also there now. But in the following document, nonetheless, there is a number series which is the same. Am I understood? So with regards to the date, I believe that that is no longer a question. Do you understand my question, Dr. Bilic?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I did notice that, Your Honour, but I also noticed that the signature that appears above the date in both documents to which Your Honour is referring appears to be the same signature, and yet for the date -- for the last document that hasn't been dealt with yet, the person who wrote it doesn't seem to have had any difficulty writing the "3". And the "3" that appears there seems to be quite different to the one that appears on the document in contention. It might be just that it's in error, but it certainly seems to me, looking at both documents, if one assumes that the signatures are the same, I don't profess to be a handwriting expert, but I do notice the stamp there. It would seem to me that one couldn't confuse a '91 with a '93.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Very well. I would like for Dr. Bilic to say something with regards to the sequence of these numbered documents. Does this mean, then, that we have the document which is at present on the ELMO, and the following document, and perhaps we might even see things more clearly if we were to see the following document. If we were to look at the actual number series that are on the upper part of that page there, you can see there is indeed a series, a number series, and there is only a difference of 21. Dr. Bilic, I think perhaps you might make a statement on this after these documents have been presented. Mr. Mikulicic, do you agree that we perhaps might deal with this issue after they have been dealt with?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, Dr. Bilic, by looking at the document which follows for Salih Hodzic and comparing the serial numbers of the two documents, the Court has observed that these could be the documents from the same series. Could you comment on this? Could it be that documents from the same series be issued one in '91 and the second in '93?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, it is impossible. The serial number could have been on the 27th of January '93, so that this document for Salih Hodzic with this serial number 16 1994 04 preceded the document issued to Hasan Pezic with the serial number 16 1994 25. In other words, that Dr. Markovic, Srdjana Markovic, could see first Salih Hodzic and then the 21st patient after him was Hasan Pezic. And I do not think that there should be any doubt that in the year it is evident that it is '93 if one looks at the serial number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Perhaps another question. Do you remember if Dr. Markovic was in the staff of the health centre in '91?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Dr. Markovic, yes. Yes, she was

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask my distinguished colleague Niemann if he is satisfied with this answer of the witness, or does he still insist on the irrelevance of the document referring to Hasan Pezic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Niemann, if I may, I should like to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, Dr. Bilic, we are now referring to documents, that is the order in which we produced them. Hasan Pezic, do you know this individual?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something from this -- about this document? It's not particularly legible, I know.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: All I can read is that this ought to be the prescription for Amilofilin. These were tablets, .25, 3 times 2, but below it I simply cannot read it. So evidently he had some respiration complaints. The diagnosis says 4 5 4 . I don't know this code.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So can you proceed then to the next document and the last one issued in the name of -- to the name of Salih Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document regarding Hasan Pezic, which has a number 25 at the end of the series, shall be given a number D18J.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, before I ask you to comment on this document, there was something that you answered which reminded me of a situation which I should like you to explain to the Honourable Court. You said, when you looked and commented on the previous documents, since the whole form had not been filled out, that it reminded you of 1993, that is the time of the conflict, and when aid, when services were extended to patients and they were not asked to submit any proof or their health insurance, that is, they did not have to produce their health insurance number. Could you explain this?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, in the normal times, and when the work is normal, then every patient, at least in our case, at the Busovaca Health Centre, had to have his health insurance card before he saw a doctor. And we needed to have all the data referring to a particular -- that particular patient, because the health centre keeps cards, keeps patient cards. When the first -- when a patient comes for the first time, then everything is put in there, that is the date, the name, the date, personal particulars, the diagnosis and so on, so forth. And for this -- and his health certificate also had to feature the number of his card. And the prescription could not be issued without it. So this prescription could be issued only at the time of the conflict in Busovaca because, in view of the situation, who would ask for the card? I mean, we had to help all patients and not ask for their papers or serial numbers or whatever. It was absurd under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, by presenting his health insurance card, the patient offers proof of his health insurance, that somebody is covered by insurance?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That it means that in this first half of '93 you simply paid no attention to the fact whether somebody was or was not covered by health insurance?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, indeed we did not. It would have been absurd under the circumstances, which were extraordinary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
