utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, can we go to this document, the document issued to the name of Salih Hodzic. Do you know this individual?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where does he come from?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: From Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you comment on this document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: We see that it was issued on the 25th of January, 1993, that Dr. Srdjana Markovic was the one who issued this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: The diagnosis 4 2 5, I do not know this code, since I am not a physician. And she prescribed Isoptin tablets, 25 milligrams, two times one; Andol tablets, one times one; Apaurin pills one time once; and the doctor emphatically stated that the patient needs treatment at home because he had a heart complaint. So he could have been brought from Kaonik and the doctor emphatically requested that be sent home for further treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Bilic, do you know of your own knowledge whether these recommendations issued by physicians about sending one for treatment, whether this was absurd, that is, whether these patients were indeed being released and sent home for treatment?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were. That is, those who were given these prescriptions, those who brought those people from Kaonik, I believe they observed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I know it because of my colleague, the previous patient, Senad Dervic, I know that he was sent home for treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. Dr. Bilic, with this I should conclude with examination. Thank you very much for your answers. Thank you very much, your Lordships.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you were at the medical centre, but you didn't practice medicine; is that what -- do I understand that to be your position?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. I worked at a medical facility, but I am not a physician. I am a pharmacist and I worked as a biochemical engineer, which was part of the diagnostic service at the health centre in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, did you just mainly involve yourself with administrative duties, or did you also become involved with the pharmacy attached to the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I worked at the health centre in Busovaca as a biochemist, which means that I was involved in laboratory diagnosis, laboratory analysis at the laboratory, which was part of the Busovaca Medical Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. And this was in addition to your administrative duties?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you -- did your either administrative duties or your professional duties at the medical centre require you to be there at the night-time, or did you work mostly during the day?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Most of the time I worked during the day, but sometimes I would also work at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when patients were brought to the hospital, I think you've testified that you saw them on a couple of occasions. Did you always see them, or was it just by chance that you happened to see patients coming to the medical centre from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't see them every time, but sometimes when I would be passing from one office to another I would see -- I would see a patient that had just been brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you said in your evidence, you spoke of food being prepared and distributed from barracks. I was just wondering if you could tell me what barracks were you referring to when you said that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I was referring to the barracks of the former JNA in Busovaca, in the place called Draga.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were these barracks occupied by the Dutch battalion, were they, or were they someone else?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, the Dutch battalion was accommodated in hotel in Busovaca, one part of the Dutch battalion, and the other part of the Dutch battalion was quartered in the high school building in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you -- were you in a position at any stage to seek assistance, medical assistance that is, from the Dutch battalion?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I believe I already mentioned that sometimes if we needed some specific medication, which we didn't have at the health centre in Busovaca, I would ask the Dutch battalion for help. In case they had that particular medication, they would always give it to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you spoke of there being a medical facility that you could refer patients to at Nova Bila. What sort of premises or what sort of facilities were available at Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: This was just one part of the newly established hospital in Nova Bila, which wasn't really a hospital. It was a church where only two surgeons were working. So you couldn't really call it a hospital. It didn't have all necessary departments. It was a war hospital, a makeshift hospital where patients from this particular area could be admitted, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I think -- were you in Busovaca just prior to the outbreak of hostilities in January of 1993? Were you still living there then or at that time were you living there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, as the sort of tensions built up, did you see troops come into the town at all, into the town of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You didn't observe any build-up of troops in the town at all?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't observe any.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You spoke of going to the Kaonik camp, the Kaonik facility, yourself on one occasion and that you are aware of the fact that your staff went there on another occasion. Was there any arrangement whereby regular visits would be paid to the camp, that you knew of?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: There were no such arrangements. We would go there upon the request of the warden of the Kaonik facility, whenever it was necessary. When we had to see a particular patient, the physicians would go there. And two occasions that I mentioned, it was just an occasion for us to see what the situation was, the epidemiological situation, not only at the prison facility but also on the territory of the Municipality of Busovaca in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If I understand your evidence, did you say that in 1992, as opposed to 1993, that Serb patients were being brought to you from the Kaonik camp? Did you say that, or was that something I misunderstood?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I don't think it was a camp. In my opinion, Kaonik was not a camp, as far as could I see. As to people who were brought in, these were just people from the Kaonik facility, people who had committed some kind of criminal offence, because we had both Croats and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. But in 1992, and we won't call it a camp, if that's not your understanding of it, but in 1992, when it was used as a prison, the people that were brought to you were mainly Serb; is that the effect of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Not mainly Serbs. There were also Croats amongst them. There were both Croats and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you understood these people in 1992 to be prisoners?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you know why, particularly the Serbs I am interested in, do you know why the Serbs were in Kaonik as prisoners in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you spoke of people wearing military clothing during the period of the war. Did you wear military clothing yourself?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what about members of your staff, did any of the doctors that worked with you, or nurses, wear military clothing?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No. Not at the Busovaca Health Centre. We had white coats, and these white coats were our uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. When did you first understand that the Kaonik facility was being used to house prisoners? When did you first understand that to occur?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: In late 1992, when they started bringing in people from Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And in late 1992 most of the conflict was between the Croatian people; Muslim people and the Serbs being on the other side. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No. In late 1992 there was no conflict between Croats and Muslims. At that time we had no such conflict in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I think you misunderstood what I said. You are absolutely right, the point is the conflict at that time, in '92, was between the Croats and Serbs, and also the Muslims and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: In Busovaca there was no such conflict between Croats and Serbs and Muslims and Serbs. There was just one occasion, there was one shelling incident when Busovaca was shelled with missiles in April 1992, when the health centre was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Now, when you went to the Kaonik facility, you saw the prisoners that were being detained there? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you knew some of the people?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: By sight, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the people that you saw there, they were, by this stage in 1993, Muslims?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were they women and children and men, or just men that you can remember seeing?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Only men were there. There were no women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And do you know why there was only men there? You may not know this.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were they of any particular age group, the men, or were they all a full range of age groups that you could see?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I believe full range of age groups. Only men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know why they were there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see any infirmary or medical sort of hospital or anything of that nature at the Kaonik facility when you went there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You didn't see any particular rooms which had been set aside for providing medical care?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I think it's obvious, because you've told us what your duties are, but just for the record, your evidence is that you'd never yourself actually carried out an examination of any of the people that had come from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, because I am not a physician.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I think you also gave evidence of the fact that the Kaonik prisoners that were brought to the medical facility, they didn't appear to be constrained or tied up in any way with handcuffs or any means; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the guards or Mr. Aleksovski, when you saw him there with prisoners, did he appear to be armed with weapons of any sort?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So I take it from that, then, that these people were not considered dangerous criminals or anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, I guess not. It was not my duty to judge what they were, whether they were criminals, whether they were dangerous or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But in charge of the facility, as you were, if they were bringing in notoriously dangerous criminals, I take it you would be concerned about your other patients, if that was the case?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, of course I would be concerned if someone is a dangerous criminal, and if he's brought to my institution without handcuffs. Of course I would be concerned for the safety of other patients and other staff who were there at the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think your evidence is that you knew some of the people, some of the Muslim people that were brought there from Kaonik. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And certainly, other than them being unfortunately involved in the conflict, there was no fear or thought in your mind of them being dangerous or notorious or anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you say that if people had developed skin disorders at the camp, you should have been informed about that. Do you remember saying something to that effect in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would have been. I should have been informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who would have informed you of that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I would have been informed by the physician who established the existence of such a skin disorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about the camp? What sort of reporting facility was put in place so that if someone became ill at the camp, how did you then get to know that that patient was ill?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, again, in my opinion, it was not a camp. For us, in order to get there, it was enough for someone from Kaonik to come and see us and to tell us that there was need for the physician to visit the facility, or we could have also been informed by phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, I take it, that the process by which you would be informed was entirely dependent upon those persons who were in charge of the camp, such as Mr. Aleksovski or the guards?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Most probably so, yes. Because we, at the medical centre, couldn't be aware of such things at the prison facility. Someone had to inform us. Someone had to tell us that there was a patient in need of care, or maybe the patient could come to the centre himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever have any visits from the International Committee of the Red Cross about patients in the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No. Not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, in your evidence you described the situation at Kaonik, so far as you were concerned, as being normal for that type of facility. And you've also corrected me for using the word "camp." What did you mean by the term "normal for that type of facility" when you said that? What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I meant that it was a facility where a large number of people were accommodated. And as for the prevailing conditions during that conflict, the situation was not good. I mean, the general situation couldn't be good at any facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You spoke of the fact that it would be contrary to medical ethics for doctors or medical staff at the Busovaca Medical Centre to discriminate on the basis of nationality. I take it, that you can't positively rule out that some members of your staff may have discriminated on the basis of nationality, but it's something that you simply didn't know about at the time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I didn't know about such cases, but I believe that there was no discrimination in respect of patients. Every patient who would come to our institution, he was simply a patient for all of us. We didn't pay attention to his ethnic background, to his name, surname, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I am quite sure that you never did, but I am just saying that if others on your staff did, it's possible it may have happened and you didn't know?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: It may have happened, but I'm sure that there were no such cases, that nobody discriminated in that sense at the health centre in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You spoke of conditions during the war, and I am quite sure they must have been very hard for everybody. But were the basic facilities available to you personally during the war? When I say basic facilities, were you able to gather enough food and to wash and tend to your personal needs like that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, I was in the same situation as other people, and I probably ate the same food at the health centre as the people at the Kaonik facility. I had soap to wash myself, and I believe the people at the Kaonik facility also had soap.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about heating?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: As far as heating is concerned, at the health centre in Busovaca we had the central heating system from before the war. We had a boiler room and we had some coal left. So we did have heating for a period of time at the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you went to Kaonik, what was the heating facilities there like? Did you make any observations about that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about -- did people appear to have sufficient blankets and bedding that you could see?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I wasn't -- I didn't see whether they had blankets or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It's a long time back, but did you notice the beds, the type of beds people were sleeping in?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. Sorry, I don't remember. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you go into -- I think you said that you went into all parts of the prison. Did you go into -- do you remember going into a large hangar type building with a lot of people in it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What do you remember seeing, in terms of the buildings that you went into?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I saw a big building, there was an entrance to that building, several rooms. There was a toilet facility next to the rooms. I can remember this much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And these rooms appeared to be divided into cells; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, they looked that way, but I -- they didn't look like real cells, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you go into -- inside of any of these cells, or did you just look at them from the outside?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I didn't go inside. I saw them from the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you don't remember a big, open hangar building with a lot of people in it at all at that stage?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see a place where people could wash their clothes and dry them?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you spoke of the toilet facilities. What was it that enabled you to differentiate between staff toilet facilities and toilet facilities of the prisoners? What enabled you to do that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, they were the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But there was nothing that permitted you to say that this was definitely a toilet for prisoners as opposed to staff; to you all the toilets looked the same? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, they looked the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you sit down and speak to any of the prisoners there at the time and ask them about their conditions?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During this particular period in time did you -- bear with me a moment. Did you know of a Dr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mohamed Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No. No. I only heard that this physician used to work in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you know that he was brought down to your medical facility during April and May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: As a doctor or as a patient?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As a doctor. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You don't recall him being brought down each -- just about every day for a two-week period? It's a long time back now, but he was collected from Vitez and brought down.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: He was not brought to the health centre. I'm sure about that. You mean to work -- that Dr. Mujezinovic would work at the health centre in Busovaca? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You don't remember?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I remember that he didn't work -- he wasn't working there, because I was there during that period. Dr. Mujezinovic from Vitez was not coming to work at the health centre in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And he's Muslim, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, by his name and surname, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You spoke of the Busovaca medical facility being the only facility in Busovaca, but wasn't there also a facility at the kindergarten?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: At the kindergarten, yes. There was one facility which was a branch of the Nova Bila Hospital which only had a few beds for patients who were able to leave the Nova Bila Hospital. There were no doctors there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And this facility at the kindergarten was for HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I believe so, but I am not sure. I don't know. I am not aware of that because I was working at the health centre, which is a separate institution. I was not working with the Nova Bila Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you're still the director of the medical centre in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And so you would have access to all the medical records that are being kept there, is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So if representatives from the office of the Prosecutor were to come and see you, you'd be able to show us those records that you keep there for this particular period?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And with these medical records, the sample group that you've brought to court with you here, what has been brought here, did you get permission from the patients to bring these documents to court?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question, I am not sure I understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The series of the documents from the hospital that we went through and have been marked as exhibits and were placed on the overhead projector, I was just asking you, did you obtain the permission of the patients to bring those records here to court?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't obtain permission from patients because these documents, the documents they received, remained at the medical centre in Busovaca. They were not in their possession. So there was no need for me to ask them to give this documentation. Because if I issue one particular prescription or document, I keep it, we keep it at the medical centre. It is never given to the patient. He gets a copy for the prescription and this other document stays here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So the information that's contained in these documents is not considered by you to be privileged medical information in other words?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I don't consider it as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now just going through these documents, and I think it might help you if you were to have access to them and to assist their Honours if we put a copy on the projector. I would like to ask you some questions about them, if I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me, but I believe we're going to be working until 1.30, perhaps we might divide that time up appropriately. Perhaps we might take a break now, unless you have a question you would like to put to the witness now. Otherwise, I think it be best see when we continue. Should we take a recess now? Very well. Let's take a fifteen minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, please resume. Wait a moment, please. (The accused entered court).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, I was about to ask you some questions about the documents that have been tendered into evidence. And perhaps if I can do them one by one, that would help. The first one, D-18/A A. If that can be placed on the overhead projector, please. Doctor, this person, Ilijaz Krivosija, did you know this person at all?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I did, yes, he was a neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what was his employment, what did he do in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I hope you'll believe me that I don't know. I think he worked for the steel works in Zenica, but I only think so, I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I take it you didn't understand him to be in any way connected with the military, the JNA or the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know how or why it was that he ended up in the Kaonik camp by any chance if he was a neighbour?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: -- to camp in my view, but I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. And just looking at the document itself, Exhibit D-18/A, and perhaps it could be displayed on the overhead projector. It probably already is. The English version of it, perhaps, we might see. Do you notice there you it says "exemption from work," presumably that means work at the Kaonik prison -- yes, by the Kaonik prison?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know, I didn't write this prescription. It was the doctor who did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You're aware, I take it, that prisoners were used for the purposes of digging trenches during that period of 1993, people who were detained at the Kaonik prison?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know the sort of work people were doing there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know it, I wasn't a doctor and I really don't know what she meant or what she told the patient. The patient never came to from me to a prison to be examined by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you'd agree with me if it were for no other reason but for general knowledge, that digging trenches would not be the sort of appropriate activity for someone with a discus hernia?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where is Dr. Mioc now?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know, believe me, I think she's in Australia. She was from Zenica, otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you'll notice that it says "sleeping on a flat bed recommended." I take it you don't know whether those sorts of facilities were available in the prison at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: About these facilities, I don't know, but I think it could be made available.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would sleeping on one of those packing racks, the racks that they use to pack boxes and things on, would that be suitable or do you think the doctor may have had in mind something a bit more elaborate than that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the doctor had in mind, but I guess a board, a wooden board would have been enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, going to the next document, Document 18/B. You'll notice that in this one it prescribes the treatment at home recommended. What is it about being treated at home that would have been better for this person than being in the Kaonik prison?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And do you know this person, Avdo Husbasic?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You notice that the tablets that have been prescribed there, are you familiar with those particular tablets?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Amilofilin tablets, two times one tablet, yes, I know that one. Ramital, I don't know, I don't know what it would be in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Ramital, R-a-m-i-t-a-l.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is that normally prescribed for?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Ramital is normally prescribed, as far as I know, for the stomach or duodenal ulcer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I notice that Dr. Petrovic is an obstetrician and gynaecologist. I take it that doctors were in somewhat short supply then, so you had to use whatever doctors that were available?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: She tried, yes, she did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where is Dr. Petrovic now?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Health centre at Busovaca. She is there right this minute, she is working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the next document, 18/C. Did you know this person, Ismet Medjuseljac?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And do you know where he came from?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And do you remember him as being a patient previously at the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And do you know whether or not he had any particular complaints prior to this?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know, I am not a doctor. And I didn't see his card.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If you look at the next one, 18/D. Again, we have this recommendation for home treatment, did you know this person, Ejub Buljina?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I think it's your evidence that these recommendations were accepted and acted upon by the prison officials at Kaonik, is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I said that, yes they did, they accepted them. And they know it about one patient for sure, but as for the others, I did not ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And obviously on this occasion only five days at home was considered the appropriate period of time for recovery?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I guess so. The doctor who treated him must have thought that that would be enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And after five days, they would be taken back to the Kaonik prison?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when they went home, I don't suppose you know whether or not they were guarded or in any way prevented from leaving the area?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And Dr. Markovic, where is Dr. Markovic now, do you know?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Dr. Markovic is in the Netherlands now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Looking at the next one, 18/E. Do you know Suad Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: By sight, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And do you know where he lived prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know the premises that he was required were to live in -- I'm sorry, I withdraw that. Do you know the place where he lived, was it an apartment block or an ordinary house or maybe you don't know?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I think he lived there in a house, in a private house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And do you know happened to him during the war?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the diagnosis there, that would be consistent, I think you said in your evidence, with a blow to the chest without fracture?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I know you've said numerous times that you're not a doctor, but it could also be consistent with being beaten?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know, it's possible, it's possible. It may be yes, it may be no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now looking at the next one 18/F, do you know of the drug Andol, A-n-d-o-l? Yes, do you know about the drug Andol?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is it normally used for?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: It can be prescribed as a pain killer or to combat fever, analgesic or for some heart complaints, better circulation, bring the fever down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you may not know what cold compresses are commonly used for?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Presumably for some inflammations or perhaps endyma or perhaps sprained joints.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Or bruising, damage to the body like that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: That too, yes, possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Looking at the next one, 18/G. I notice this one says swelling in front of the left ear and has an earache. The recommended therapy and prescriptions there suggest that there may have been an infection in the ear, is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I don't think there was an infection. I say I am not a doctor, but I think this is diagnosis for an inflammation of the middle ear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And obviously the doctor didn't consider draughts, that the patient would be able to kept out of the draft or be kept warm at Kaonik because they're prescribed different at home?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. She must have decided that that was the best thing for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I suppose again it might be -- and if you don't know, just say you don't know because I know you have said that you're not a medical practitioner, but I am just seeing how much you can assist me. The swelling to the left ear, could be the result of being hit or struck on the head? You don't rule out that possibility?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, one can't rule it out. But it could be the result of inflammation that it swells because it is inflammed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Which inflammation could well follow being struck on the head?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. It could be, but not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now going to D-18/H. This patient -- do you know this person at all?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And how well do you know the person?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: As well as one can know one's associates, one's business associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And have you known this person to be generally in good health when you knew him prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No, he's always had problems. He had an ulcer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I take it that if one did have a very serious ulcer and were placed in adverse conditions and in a prison, that that could exacerbate the problem?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: It could, it could exacerbate it if there really was a disease of some kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, just looking at Exhibit D-18/I for a moment. Do you notice the signature of the treating doctor here?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And who is he, what's his or her name?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Dr. Nada Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I think we asked you where Dr. Petrovic was, did you say the Netherlands?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: She's at Busovaca in the health centre, working.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, just looking at -- just moving on to the last one, 18/K, the very last one. Now, again you can only tell us so much, I know, because you are not the doctor that wrote this, but it talks about treatment at home absolutely necessary, because this patient has a bad heart condition. So, again, I think you'd agree with me that, obviously, the prescribing physician didn't consider that the conditions at the Kaonik Prison were in any way suitable for this person.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, the doctor must have thought that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That would have included the requirement of people to do physical labour, such as dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I guess so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the doctor is very clearly saying here that there is no choice in the matter, that it's absolutely necessary that the patient go home? We didn't get your answer, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the doctor thought that the patient should be at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the person, Salih Hodzic, do you know Salih Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: I do by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know this person to have a heart condition?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And is it well-known in Busovaca that he has a heart condition?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't common knowledge. I mean, not everybody knew what everybody else suffered from, but the majority of patients, because Busovaca is small, of course we all knew them. We knew most of the patients and the patient himself would say, if I met an acquaintance, he would say, "Oh, yes, this one has this and that disorder and the diagnosis was such and such." So it may not be general knowledge, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How old was Salih Hodzic, approximately? I know you wouldn't know his precise date of birth, but approximately.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately, I don't know. I really don't. But I think he could be around 50 something, 55 maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you didn't understand him to be part of the military of Busovaca with his heart condition?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Niemann. Mr. Mikulicic, do you have any questions, any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO NAVIA
utterances.text: Doctor, had the ambulances, I mean the health centre ambulances, identification as medical vehicles, such as Red Cross signs or something like that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they did have signs, Red Cross signs, and it was written on each of them "Busovaca Health Centre."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Dr. Bilic, this is the end of your testimony here before the International Criminal Tribunal. The Chamber has no further questions to put to you, so we like to thank you for coming and appearing, and we wish you a pleasant trip back to your country. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: For the record, the question that was put by the Trial Chamber was not by Judge Vohrah, but Judge Nieto Navia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: For the French translation, it was indeed Judge Nieto Navia. Mr. Mikulicic, it is now 1.00, 1.15. Is it worth it for us all now to proceed with the next testimony or should we leave this for tomorrow, because we only have 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO NAVIA
utterances.text: For the record, the clarification was made by Judge Vohrah and not by the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We always try to arrive at the truth. Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence also believes that the next witness should not be interrupted in his testimony. Therefore, we would like to put him tomorrow morning. We should, therefore, from our point of view, finish today, and let the witness begin his testimony tomorrow morning. But before we rise, we would like the documents identified as 18A to 18K be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, no objection, I see. Therefore, it should be admitted. Now, following the proposal that has been made, I believe we are all in agreement that we can end today's session now and that we will meet tomorrow at 9 a.m. Have a pleasant afternoon to you all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
